Endorsement: Voters should support the Measure M bond to fix Gilroy schools (https://www.mercurynews.com/2026/10/29/endorsement-voters-should-support-the-measure-m-bond-to-fix-gilroy-schools/)
Those county-run systems expect to collectively lose more than a billion dollars annually. Notably, while our systems and residents are scrambling to survive, rural America is receiving a $50 billion lifeline from House Republicans and President Trump to protect their health care systems.
Proposition 40 was written to prop up this state’s safety net in the face of these devastating cuts.
However, this measure is the wrong solution to a real problem.
We advise California voters to reject short-sighted, self-sabotaging Proposition 40.
And we recommend they reject equally myopic Propositions 41 and 42 — countermeasures that would not only nullify the billionaires tax but senselessly shackle the state’s fiscal future.
Killing Golden Goose
Proposition 40 risks long-term pain for short-term gain. It’s the ballot equivalent of eating your seed corn.
Here’s how it would work:
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% levy on the net worth of billionaires who were residents of California on January 1. The tax would be due next year, but the state’s 250 or so billionaires could spread the payments out over five years.
Ninety percent of the revenues raised — estimated anywhere between $40 billion to $100 billion, depending on the expert — would fund health care services. The rest would go toward education and food assistance and administration.
What distinguishes this tax isn’t just that it’s targeting a very base of extremely high-net worth individuals but also that it applies retroactively and taxes wealth, not income.
Wealth taxes are unpopular with many economists, including liberal ones, for several reasons:
They can force the sale of productive assets (e.g. stock shares, patents, copyrights, farmland, etc). They’re difficult to administer because determining the value of some intangible assets, unlike income, is more art than a science. And most injuriously, they can encourage capital flight, especially when executed by a state acting alone.
To be sure, the capital hasn’t fled California yet, but the capitalists have been.
Founders of some of Silicon Valley’s largest companies, including Sergey Brin, Larry Page, Peter Thiel, Mark Zuckerberg and Travis Kalanick, have changed their residencies or announced plans to cut ties with the state in one way or another.
What makes Proposition 40 so dangerously self-destructive is California’s extraordinary dependence upon taxing high-income earners. Over the last two decades, the top 1% of earners have paid approximately 45% of the state’s income taxes.
For that reason, the state’s most respected, nonpartisan authority on policy, the Legislative Analyst’s Office, forecasts short-term benefits but long-term costs:
California will “probably collect tens of billions of dollars from the wealth tax,” according to the LAO. But those gains would likely be temporary.
That’s because the LAO worries that “billionaires may respond to a new wealth tax in ways that reduce their income tax payments. For example, some billionaires may decide to leave California. The income taxes they currently pay to the state also would go away.”
In fact, the LAO projects that billionaires leaving the state would reduce the state’s General Fund revenues by “less than a billion per year.”
But the union that pushed this proposition — Services Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West — wants to gamble.
Its leaders created this to help themselves first and foremost, even at the expense of their typical allies. Opposition to this proposition includes the California Teachers Association, the Association of California School Administrators and the California Professional Firefighters, among several other public and private sector unions. These unions know they’ll suffer when the state’s General Fund takes a hit.
Even the liberal governor of this state is fiercely opposed.
“We can’t let a single advocacy organization, however well-intentioned, write the state’s tax code on its own terms,” said Gov. Gavin Newsom.
We couldn’t agree more.
Self-shackling
To counter Proposition 40, Building a Better California — a political action committee formed earlier this year and backed by Silicon Valley billionaires including Sergey Brin, Vinod Khosla and Eric Scmidt — created two countermeasures, Propositions 41 and 42.
If either Proposition 41 or 42 receives more votes than Proposition 40, the billionaires tax won’t take effect.
The problem is that these two propositions would do far more than nullify the billionaires tax. They would tie the hands of the state far into the future in ways we cannot abide.
Proposition 41
This initiative’s requirement for more audits could be valuable. It would mandate that the State Auditor scrutinize special taxes before they appear on the ballot as well as ongoing programs funded by special taxes. The LAO sees possible savings if the auditor’s recommendations are followed.
However, the problem with Proposition 41 is its second provision. It would prevent any new special taxes from being excluded from the “Gann Limit” — a strict state spending cap enacted in 1979. That means that voters could approve a new tax to address a pressing public need, only to discover that the state cannot spend the money it collects without being constrained by a constitutional limit written half a century ago.

How the Gann Limit Threatens Ongoing Investments for Californians
December 2022 | By Kayla Kitson (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/kayla-kitson/), Scott Graves (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/scott-graves/), and Jonathan Kaplan
Print Q&A
Building a just and equitable California for every person no matter their race, ethnicity, gender, age, or zip code requires investments to create health, housing, economic, and educational opportunities. But an archaic spending limit approved by some California voters under a 1979 ballot measure challenges our state’s ability to meet the ongoing needs of Californians. Known by many names — the spending cap, appropriations limit, or Gann Limit — this convoluted budget constraint blocks the state’s ability to build a better and more equitable future.
This Gann Limit Q&A addresses top questions on the spending cap and why California leaders and voters need to rethink the disco-era measure to create healthy, thriving communities for all Californians.
Jump To:
What are the origins of the Gann Limit?
How does the Gann Limit work?
Why does this spending limit matter today?
How does the Gann Limit threaten ongoing investments to help Californians thrive?
Does the Gann Limit affect local governments and school districts?
What can state leaders do about the Gann Limit?
1. What are the origins of the Gann Limit?
The Gann Limit is a constitutional spending cap approved by voters via Proposition 4 in a 1979 special election. Prop. 4 emerged from California’s anti-tax movement of the 1970s. The measure’s key proponent, Paul Gann, also co-authored Prop. 13 — the 1978 initiative that severely restricted property taxes and drastically limited the ability of local jurisdictions to raise revenues for education and community services such as libraries, parks, and fire protection.
Prop. 4 and Prop. 13 were approved by a majority-white electorate during a time when the state’s population was becoming more diverse and white Californians’ support for robust public services was in decline (https://stateofresistancebook.com/articles/prop13).
2. How does the Gann Limit work?
The Gann Limit applies to both state spending and, as explained in question #5, spending by local governments and school districts. At the state level, the limit is based on California’s 1978-79 spending level, which is then adjusted each year for changes in population and per capita personal income. In essence, the Gann Limit enshrined into the state’s Constitution the budget priorities of the late 1970s — even though the needs of Californians have dramatically changed since the disco era.
If revenues exceed the limit over a two-year period, state policymakers must provide half of the revenue over that limit to taxpayers and the other half to K-14 education. Policymakers have some discretion over how to distribute the portion going to taxpayers. In contrast, the portion going to K-14 education must be distributed on a per-pupil basis, which is an inequitable approach that treats all schools the same regardless of their students’ needs.
Alternatively, policymakers have limited options to structure budgets to avoid going over the limit, as explained in question #6. In either case, state leaders lose the flexibility to spend revenues in ways that address critical ongoing needs of Californians, including health care, child care, and housing assistance. For an in-depth explanation of how the Gann Limit works, see this April 2021 report (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4416) by the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
3. Why does this spending limit matter today?
For most of the last two decades, state revenues were far enough below the Gann Limit that it did not have a significant impact on budgeting decisions. However, when the state’s revenues grow faster than population and personal income, as they have in recent years, the Gann Limit comes into play and dictates how a large share of the budget can be spent.
Big revenue gains primarily come from personal income taxes paid by high-income households, who experience much faster income growth than the typical Californian, and who pay higher tax rates under the state’s progressive income tax system (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/californias-tax-revenue-system-isnt-fair-for-all/). While there will be years when the Gann Limit is less of a factor in state budget decisions, over the long run the spending cap will likely continue to impose budget constraints to the extent that state revenues grow faster than the limit itself, as has been the case historically (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4646).
4. How does the Gann Limit threaten ongoing investments to help Californians thrive?
The Gann Limit challenges California’s ability to maintain current service levels and to raise revenues to make bold new investments to help more Californians prosper.
The Gann Limit is just one of several budget formulas in the state Constitution (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/dollars-and-democracy-a-guide-to-the-state-budget-process-2019/) that dictate how revenues can be spent. Prop. 98, approved by voters in 1988, creates a guaranteed annual minimum funding level for K-14 education. Prop. 2 (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-2-should-california-prioritize-paying-down-debt-and-significantly-change-state-budget-reserve-policies/), approved by voters in 2014, requires the state to direct some revenues to paying down debts and adding to the state’s main budget reserve (the Budget Stabilization Account). When revenues exceed the Gann Limit, each dollar above the limit must meet all three requirements: Gann, Prop. 98, and Prop. 2. This means that each $1 of “excess” revenue results in more than $1 in state budget obligations (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4515). Addressing all three obligations could force state leaders to cut public services outside of K-14 education, such as health care, child care, and cash assistance as well as the state university systems.
In addition to undercutting the state’s ability to support current service levels, the spending cap, if left unchanged, will undermine efforts to raise enough revenue to fund significant new ongoing investments to help all Californians thrive. These include investments to expand affordable child care (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/moving-beyond-relief-for-california-care/), increase pay for child care providers (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/californias-subsidized-child-care-providers-are-overdue-for-pay-raise/), and adequately address the homelessness (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/who-is-experiencing-homelessness-in-california/) and affordable housing (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/who-is-experiencing-housing-hardship-in-california/) crises.
Cutting critical services and failing to address the biggest challenges facing the state would significantly harm Californians with low incomes who may not be able to make ends meet without the help of public supports. Many Californians of color are at particular risk because of historical and ongoing discrimination that has often limited them to low-paying, undervalued jobs and blocked them from opportunities to build wealth.
5. Does the Gann Limit affect local governments and school districts?
The Gann Limit generally applies to local governments — cities, counties, and special districts — as well as to K-12 and community college districts, all of which could be impacted in the years to come. Many school districts regularly exceed their spending caps, although the state is currently able to provide relief to these districts by counting certain district expenditures toward the state’s own limit. In general, few cities or counties are currently at risk of exceeding their limits.
However, in future years, the Gann Limit could put pressure on local budgets, particularly for cities and counties that seek revenue increases to bolster local services like affordable housing, health care, parks, and libraries.
6. What can state leaders do about the Gann Limit?
State leaders have some ability to structure budgets to avoid exceeding the limit in the near term. For example, they can spend more on things that are excluded from the limit, such as:
infrastructure projects, including housing;
emergency response;
tax refunds;
some transfers of state funds to local governments; and
spending to comply with court and federal mandates.
Policymakers can also reduce revenues to avoid going over the limit, such as by expanding tax credits like the California Earned Income Tax Credit and Young Child Tax Credit (https://calbudgetcenter.org/series/what-is-the-california-earned-income-tax-credit/).
Finally, some of the Gann Limit rules are spelled out in state statute rather than in the state Constitution. In these cases, lawmakers have limited opportunities to change the law to ease some Gann Limit pressures. For example, state leaders made some changes in the 2021-22 (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4449) and 2022-23 (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4631) state budgets to avoid exceeding the limit, including allowing more flexibility in deciding whether to count state funding for local governments under the state or local limits.
However, in the long run, the Gann Limit’s restrictive rules may jeopardize existing services and many kinds of ongoing expenditures, such as big new investments in affordable child care or health care.
Even though a period of weak revenue growth may temporarily keep the state under the spending cap, the Gann Limit will roar back to life when revenues pick up again. In order to address the long-run threats posed by the limit, state leaders should ask California voters to change the state Constitution to modify or eliminate the spending cap. This would allow the state to both support the rising costs of current services and leave room for significant new ongoing investments to address the critical needs of Californians.

Report
How the Gann Limit Threatens Ongoing Investments for Californians
December 2022 | By Kayla Kitson (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/kayla-kitson/), Scott Graves (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/scott-graves/), and Jonathan Kaplan
Print Q&A
Building a just and equitable California for every person no matter their race, ethnicity, gender, age, or zip code requires investments to create health, housing, economic, and educational opportunities. But an archaic spending limit approved by some California voters under a 1979 ballot measure challenges our state’s ability to meet the ongoing needs of Californians. Known by many names — the spending cap, appropriations limit, or Gann Limit — this convoluted budget constraint blocks the state’s ability to build a better and more equitable future.
This Gann Limit Q&A addresses top questions on the spending cap and why California leaders and voters need to rethink the disco-era measure to create healthy, thriving communities for all Californians.
Jump To:
What are the origins of the Gann Limit?
How does the Gann Limit work?
Why does this spending limit matter today?
How does the Gann Limit threaten ongoing investments to help Californians thrive?
Does the Gann Limit affect local governments and school districts?
What can state leaders do about the Gann Limit?
1. What are the origins of the Gann Limit?
The Gann Limit is a constitutional spending cap approved by voters via Proposition 4 in a 1979 special election. Prop. 4 emerged from California’s anti-tax movement of the 1970s. The measure’s key proponent, Paul Gann, also co-authored Prop. 13 — the 1978 initiative that severely restricted property taxes and drastically limited the ability of local jurisdictions to raise revenues for education and community services such as libraries, parks, and fire protection.
Prop. 4 and Prop. 13 were approved by a majority-white electorate during a time when the state’s population was becoming more diverse and white Californians’ support for robust public services was in decline (https://stateofresistancebook.com/articles/prop13).
2. How does the Gann Limit work?
The Gann Limit applies to both state spending and, as explained in question #5, spending by local governments and school districts. At the state level, the limit is based on California’s 1978-79 spending level, which is then adjusted each year for changes in population and per capita personal income. In essence, the Gann Limit enshrined into the state’s Constitution the budget priorities of the late 1970s — even though the needs of Californians have dramatically changed since the disco era.
If revenues exceed the limit over a two-year period, state policymakers must provide half of the revenue over that limit to taxpayers and the other half to K-14 education. Policymakers have some discretion over how to distribute the portion going to taxpayers. In contrast, the portion going to K-14 education must be distributed on a per-pupil basis, which is an inequitable approach that treats all schools the same regardless of their students’ needs.
Alternatively, policymakers have limited options to structure budgets to avoid going over the limit, as explained in question #6. In either case, state leaders lose the flexibility to spend revenues in ways that address critical ongoing needs of Californians, including health care, child care, and housing assistance. For an in-depth explanation of how the Gann Limit works, see this April 2021 report (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4416) by the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
3. Why does this spending limit matter today?
For most of the last two decades, state revenues were far enough below the Gann Limit that it did not have a significant impact on budgeting decisions. However, when the state’s revenues grow faster than population and personal income, as they have in recent years, the Gann Limit comes into play and dictates how a large share of the budget can be spent.
Big revenue gains primarily come from personal income taxes paid by high-income households, who experience much faster income growth than the typical Californian, and who pay higher tax rates under the state’s progressive income tax system (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/californias-tax-revenue-system-isnt-fair-for-all/). While there will be years when the Gann Limit is less of a factor in state budget decisions, over the long run the spending cap will likely continue to impose budget constraints to the extent that state revenues grow faster than the limit itself, as has been the case historically (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4646).
4. How does the Gann Limit threaten ongoing investments to help Californians thrive?
The Gann Limit challenges California’s ability to maintain current service levels and to raise revenues to make bold new investments to help more Californians prosper.
The Gann Limit is just one of several budget formulas in the state Constitution (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/dollars-and-democracy-a-guide-to-the-state-budget-process-2019/) that dictate how revenues can be spent. Prop. 98, approved by voters in 1988, creates a guaranteed annual minimum funding level for K-14 education. Prop. 2 (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-2-should-california-prioritize-paying-down-debt-and-significantly-change-state-budget-reserve-policies/), approved by voters in 2014, requires the state to direct some revenues to paying down debts and adding to the state’s main budget reserve (the Budget Stabilization Account). When revenues exceed the Gann Limit, each dollar above the limit must meet all three requirements: Gann, Prop. 98, and Prop. 2. This means that each $1 of “excess” revenue results in more than $1 in state budget obligations (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4515). Addressing all three obligations could force state leaders to cut public services outside of K-14 education, such as health care, child care, and cash assistance as well as the state university systems.
In addition to undercutting the state’s ability to support current service levels, the spending cap, if left unchanged, will undermine efforts to raise enough revenue to fund significant new ongoing investments to help all Californians thrive. These include investments to expand affordable child care (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/moving-beyond-relief-for-california-care/), increase pay for child care providers (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/californias-subsidized-child-care-providers-are-overdue-for-pay-raise/), and adequately address the homelessness (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/who-is-experiencing-homelessness-in-california/) and affordable housing (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/who-is-experiencing-housing-hardship-in-california/) crises.
Cutting critical services and failing to address the biggest challenges facing the state would significantly harm Californians with low incomes who may not be able to make ends meet without the help of public supports. Many Californians of color are at particular risk because of historical and ongoing discrimination that has often limited them to low-paying, undervalued jobs and blocked them from opportunities to build wealth.
5. Does the Gann Limit affect local governments and school districts?
The Gann Limit generally applies to local governments — cities, counties, and special districts — as well as to K-12 and community college districts, all of which could be impacted in the years to come. Many school districts regularly exceed their spending caps, although the state is currently able to provide relief to these districts by counting certain district expenditures toward the state’s own limit. In general, few cities or counties are currently at risk of exceeding their limits.
However, in future years, the Gann Limit could put pressure on local budgets, particularly for cities and counties that seek revenue increases to bolster local services like affordable housing, health care, parks, and libraries.
6. What can state leaders do about the Gann Limit?
State leaders have some ability to structure budgets to avoid exceeding the limit in the near term. For example, they can spend more on things that are excluded from the limit, such as:
infrastructure projects, including housing;
emergency response;
tax refunds;
some transfers of state funds to local governments; and
spending to comply with court and federal mandates.
Policymakers can also reduce revenues to avoid going over the limit, such as by expanding tax credits like the California Earned Income Tax Credit and Young Child Tax Credit (https://calbudgetcenter.org/series/what-is-the-california-earned-income-tax-credit/).
Finally, some of the Gann Limit rules are spelled out in state statute rather than in the state Constitution. In these cases, lawmakers have limited opportunities to change the law to ease some Gann Limit pressures. For example, state leaders made some changes in the 2021-22 (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4449) and 2022-23 (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4631) state budgets to avoid exceeding the limit, including allowing more flexibility in deciding whether to count state funding for local governments under the state or local limits.
However, in the long run, the Gann Limit’s restrictive rules may jeopardize existing services and many kinds of ongoing expenditures, such as big new investments in affordable child care or health care.
Even though a period of weak revenue growth may temporarily keep the state under the spending cap, the Gann Limit will roar back to life when revenues pick up again. In order to address the long-run threats posed by the limit, state leaders should ask California voters to change the state Constitution to modify or eliminate the spending cap. This would allow the state to both support the rising costs of current services and leave room for significant new ongoing investments to address the critical needs of Californians.

How the Gann Limit Threatens Ongoing Investments for Californians
December 2022 | By Kayla Kitson (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/kayla-kitson/), Scott Graves (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/scott-graves/), and Jonathan Kaplan
Print Q&A
Building a just and equitable California for every person no matter their race, ethnicity, gender, age, or zip code requires investments to create health, housing, economic, and educational opportunities. But an archaic spending limit approved by some California voters under a 1979 ballot measure challenges our state’s ability to meet the ongoing needs of Californians. Known by many names — the spending cap, appropriations limit, or Gann Limit — this convoluted budget constraint blocks the state’s ability to build a better and more equitable future.
This Gann Limit Q&A addresses top questions on the spending cap and why California leaders and voters need to rethink the disco-era measure to create healthy, thriving communities for all Californians.

1. What are the origins of the Gann Limit?
The Gann Limit is a constitutional spending cap approved by voters via Proposition 4 in a 1979 special election. Prop. 4 emerged from California’s anti-tax movement of the 1970s. The measure’s key proponent, Paul Gann, also co-authored Prop. 13 — the 1978 initiative that severely restricted property taxes and drastically limited the ability of local jurisdictions to raise revenues for education and community services such as libraries, parks, and fire protection.
Prop. 4 and Prop. 13 were approved by a majority-white electorate during a time when the state’s population was becoming more diverse and white Californians’ support for robust public services was in decline (https://stateofresistancebook.com/articles/prop13).
2. How does the Gann Limit work?
The Gann Limit applies to both state spending and, as explained in question #5, spending by local governments and school districts. At the state level, the limit is based on California’s 1978-79 spending level, which is then adjusted each year for changes in population and per capita personal income. In essence, the Gann Limit enshrined into the state’s Constitution the budget priorities of the late 1970s — even though the needs of Californians have dramatically changed since the disco era.
If revenues exceed the limit over a two-year period, state policymakers must provide half of the revenue over that limit to taxpayers and the other half to K-14 education. Policymakers have some discretion over how to distribute the portion going to taxpayers. In contrast, the portion going to K-14 education must be distributed on a per-pupil basis, which is an inequitable approach that treats all schools the same regardless of their students’ needs.
Alternatively, policymakers have limited options to structure budgets to avoid going over the limit, as explained in question #6. In either case, state leaders lose the flexibility to spend revenues in ways that address critical ongoing needs of Californians, including health care, child care, and housing assistance. For an in-depth explanation of how the Gann Limit works, see this April 2021 report (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4416) by the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
3. Why does this spending limit matter today?
For most of the last two decades, state revenues were far enough below the Gann Limit that it did not have a significant impact on budgeting decisions. However, when the state’s revenues grow faster than population and personal income, as they have in recent years, the Gann Limit comes into play and dictates how a large share of the budget can be spent.
Big revenue gains primarily come from personal income taxes paid by high-income households, who experience much faster income growth than the typical Californian, and who pay higher tax rates under the state’s progressive income tax system (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/californias-tax-revenue-system-isnt-fair-for-all/). While there will be years when the Gann Limit is less of a factor in state budget decisions, over the long run the spending cap will likely continue to impose budget constraints to the extent that state revenues grow faster than the limit itself, as has been the case historically (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4646).
4. How does the Gann Limit threaten ongoing investments to help Californians thrive?
The Gann Limit challenges California’s ability to maintain current service levels and to raise revenues to make bold new investments to help more Californians prosper.
The Gann Limit is just one of several budget formulas in the state Constitution (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/dollars-and-democracy-a-guide-to-the-state-budget-process-2019/) that dictate how revenues can be spent. Prop. 98, approved by voters in 1988, creates a guaranteed annual minimum funding level for K-14 education. Prop. 2 (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-2-should-california-prioritize-paying-down-debt-and-significantly-change-state-budget-reserve-policies/), approved by voters in 2014, requires the state to direct some revenues to paying down debts and adding to the state’s main budget reserve (the Budget Stabilization Account). When revenues exceed the Gann Limit, each dollar above the limit must meet all three requirements: Gann, Prop. 98, and Prop. 2. This means that each $1 of “excess” revenue results in more than $1 in state budget obligations (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4515). Addressing all three obligations could force state leaders to cut public services outside of K-14 education, such as health care, child care, and cash assistance as well as the state university systems.
In addition to undercutting the state’s ability to support current service levels, the spending cap, if left unchanged, will undermine efforts to raise enough revenue to fund significant new ongoing investments to help all Californians thrive. These include investments to expand affordable child care (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/moving-beyond-relief-for-california-care/), increase pay for child care providers (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/californias-subsidized-child-care-providers-are-overdue-for-pay-raise/), and adequately address the homelessness (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/who-is-experiencing-homelessness-in-california/) and affordable housing (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/who-is-experiencing-housing-hardship-in-california/) crises.
Cutting critical services and failing to address the biggest challenges facing the state would significantly harm Californians with low incomes who may not be able to make ends meet without the help of public supports. Many Californians of color are at particular risk because of historical and ongoing discrimination that has often limited them to low-paying, undervalued jobs and blocked them from opportunities to build wealth.
5. Does the Gann Limit affect local governments and school districts?
The Gann Limit generally applies to local governments — cities, counties, and special districts — as well as to K-12 and community college districts, all of which could be impacted in the years to come. Many school districts regularly exceed their spending caps, although the state is currently able to provide relief to these districts by counting certain district expenditures toward the state’s own limit. In general, few cities or counties are currently at risk of exceeding their limits.
However, in future years, the Gann Limit could put pressure on local budgets, particularly for cities and counties that seek revenue increases to bolster local services like affordable housing, health care, parks, and libraries.
6. What can state leaders do about the Gann Limit?
State leaders have some ability to structure budgets to avoid exceeding the limit in the near term. For example, they can spend more on things that are excluded from the limit, such as:
infrastructure projects, including housing;
emergency response;
tax refunds;
some transfers of state funds to local governments; and
spending to comply with court and federal mandates.
Policymakers can also reduce revenues to avoid going over the limit, such as by expanding tax credits like the California Earned Income Tax Credit and Young Child Tax Credit (https://calbudgetcenter.org/series/what-is-the-california-earned-income-tax-credit/).
Finally, some of the Gann Limit rules are spelled out in state statute rather than in the state Constitution. In these cases, lawmakers have limited opportunities to change the law to ease some Gann Limit pressures. For example, state leaders made some changes in the 2021-22 (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4449) and 2022-23 (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4631) state budgets to avoid exceeding the limit, including allowing more flexibility in deciding whether to count state funding for local governments under the state or local limits.
However, in the long run, the Gann Limit’s restrictive rules may jeopardize existing services and many kinds of ongoing expenditures, such as big new investments in affordable child care or health care.
Even though a period of weak revenue growth may temporarily keep the state under the spending cap, the Gann Limit will roar back to life when revenues pick up again. In order to address the long-run threats posed by the limit, state leaders should ask California voters to change the state Constitution to modify or eliminate the spending cap. This would allow the state to both support the rising costs of current services and leave room for significant new ongoing investments to address the critical needs of Californians.

Endorsement: Prop 41 is a cynical poison pill. And it isn’t the only one on California’s ballot
Prop 41 is one of two attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the infamous billionaire wealth tax.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 29, 2026
It wouldn’t be a California election without a few petty, revenge-motivated ballot measures.
Proposition 41 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop41-text-proposed-laws.pdf) is one of two poison pill attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the infamous billionaire wealth tax. The measure explicitly states that even if Prop 40 passes, it would be nullified if Prop 41 or its cousin initiative Prop 42 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-proposition-42-taxes-22449389.php) pass with a larger number of votes.
Backed by Building a Better California, a political action committee largely funded by billionaire Google cofounder Sergey Brin (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-california-pac-22442333.php), Prop 41 would require new special taxes that raise money for specific purposes to adhere to state spending rules, while mandating regular audits of the programs they fund.
What’s so bad about ensuring California spends tax revenue wisely?

Well, nothing — if that’s what the measure actually does. But it’s a cheap ruse to nullify Prop 40.
The measure targets an obscure — but extremely consequential — spending rule embedded in California’s Constitution.
Known as the Gann Limit (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4416), that rule prevents the state from spending more money per taxpayer than it did in 1979 — the year voters approved the measure — once adjusted for inflation. Any money the state collects over the limit must be either refunded to taxpayers or spent on certain purposes, such as infrastructure or education.

Prop 41 would prohibit any state tax taking effect on or after Jan. 1, 2026 from sidestepping those requirements. That would neuter Prop 40, which explicitly exempts its one-time 5% wealth tax on billionaires from the Gann Limit to backfill federal healthcare cuts.
Loren Kaye, former president of a California Chamber of Commerce-affiliated think tank and a Prop 41 supporter, told us in an endorsement interview that the measure establishes a “level playing field so that everybody is similarly affected once you reach the limit.”
We agree that budget carveouts generally aren’t a good idea. But the Gann Limit isn’t sacrosanct; there are perfectly legitimate reasons for excluding certain revenues from its rules.
Consider California’s Hospital Quality Assurance Fee Program (https://www.dhcs.ca.gov/providers-partners/hospital-quality-assurance-fee-program-hqaf/), which charges hospitals a fee to unlock matching federal healthcare funds and improve services for low-income patients. These funds are currently exempt from the Gann Limit (https://funds.dof.ca.gov/app/download/3158) — a provision voters approved when they green-lighted Prop 52 in 2016 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=52&year=2016).
But the federal government, which has to approve the tax, could easily demand changes to its structure. If that were to happen and Prop 41 passes, the hospital fee program could arguably be considered a “new” special tax — and thus be subject to the Gann Limit, diverting money away from hospitals, argued David Gamage, a University of Missouri School of Law professor and Prop 41 opponent.

California’s financial regulations are impossibly complex after decades of ballot-box budgeting. Adding another restriction is only bound to make things worse.
Meanwhile, Prop 41’s audit requirements are, as Darien Shanske, a UC Davis School of Law professor and Prop 41 opponent, put it, meant to be “the chocolate coating that’s supposed to attract people.”
But they’re largely redundant and would decrease efficiency.
Prop 41 requires the state auditor to evaluate programs that will receive funding from new citizen-proposed special taxes and include its findings in the official voter information guide. But the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office already assesses each ballot initiative’s fiscal and practical impact (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop41-110326.pdf) — including at the 25% signature-gathering threshold Prop 41 identifies — and those analyses are included in the voter guide.
The measure’s ongoing audit requirement could also be counterproductive; tax measures typically contain accountability provisions, and adding an untold number of audits to the already overworked auditor’s office could distract from other critical investigations. Furthermore, Prop 41 directs the state auditor’s office to find 10% annual savings in program costs, which is arbitrary and dilutes the office’s independence.

Endorsement: Prop 41 is a cynical poison pill. And it isn’t the only one on California’s ballot
Prop 41 is one of two attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the infamous billionaire wealth tax.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 29, 2026
It wouldn’t be a California election without a few petty, revenge-motivated ballot measures.
Proposition 41 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop41-text-proposed-laws.pdf) is one of two poison pill attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the infamous billionaire wealth tax. The measure explicitly states that even if Prop 40 passes, it would be nullified if Prop 41 or its cousin initiative Prop 42 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-proposition-42-taxes-22449389.php) pass with a larger number of votes.
Backed by Building a Better California, a political action committee largely funded by billionaire Google cofounder Sergey Brin (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-california-pac-22442333.php), Prop 41 would require new special taxes that raise money for specific purposes to adhere to state spending rules, while mandating regular audits of the programs they fund.
What’s so bad about ensuring California spends tax revenue wisely?

Well, nothing — if that’s what the measure actually does. But it’s a cheap ruse to nullify Prop 40.
The measure targets an obscure — but extremely consequential — spending rule embedded in California’s Constitution.
Known as the Gann Limit (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4416), that rule prevents the state from spending more money per taxpayer than it did in 1979 — the year voters approved the measure — once adjusted for inflation. Any money the state collects over the limit must be either refunded to taxpayers or spent on certain purposes, such as infrastructure or education.

Prop 41 would prohibit any state tax taking effect on or after Jan. 1, 2026 from sidestepping those requirements. That would neuter Prop 40, which explicitly exempts its one-time 5% wealth tax on billionaires from the Gann Limit to backfill federal healthcare cuts.
Loren Kaye, former president of a California Chamber of Commerce-affiliated think tank and a Prop 41 supporter, told us in an endorsement interview that the measure establishes a “level playing field so that everybody is similarly affected once you reach the limit.”
We agree that budget carveouts generally aren’t a good idea. But the Gann Limit isn’t sacrosanct; there are perfectly legitimate reasons for excluding certain revenues from its rules.
Consider California’s Hospital Quality Assurance Fee Program (https://www.dhcs.ca.gov/providers-partners/hospital-quality-assurance-fee-program-hqaf/), which charges hospitals a fee to unlock matching federal healthcare funds and improve services for low-income patients. These funds are currently exempt from the Gann Limit (https://funds.dof.ca.gov/app/download/3158) — a provision voters approved when they green-lighted Prop 52 in 2016 (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=52&year=2016).
But the federal government, which has to approve the tax, could easily demand changes to its structure. If that were to happen and Prop 41 passes, the hospital fee program could arguably be considered a “new” special tax — and thus be subject to the Gann Limit, diverting money away from hospitals, argued David Gamage, a University of Missouri School of Law professor and Prop 41 opponent.

California’s financial regulations are impossibly complex after decades of ballot-box budgeting. Adding another restriction is only bound to make things worse.
Meanwhile, Prop 41’s audit requirements are, as Darien Shanske, a UC Davis School of Law professor and Prop 41 opponent, put it, meant to be “the chocolate coating that’s supposed to attract people.”
But they’re largely redundant and would decrease efficiency.
Prop 41 requires the state auditor to evaluate programs that will receive funding from new citizen-proposed special taxes and include its findings in the official voter information guide. But the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office already assesses each ballot initiative’s fiscal and practical impact (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop41-110326.pdf) — including at the 25% signature-gathering threshold Prop 41 identifies — and those analyses are included in the voter guide.
The measure’s ongoing audit requirement could also be counterproductive; tax measures typically contain accountability provisions, and adding an untold number of audits to the already overworked auditor’s office could distract from other critical investigations. Furthermore, Prop 41 directs the state auditor’s office to find 10% annual savings in program costs, which is arbitrary and dilutes the office’s independence.

Successive waves of federal cuts to California’s safety net are hitting our shores — and hospitals.
H.R. 1 (aka the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act”), the spending plan written by House Republicans and signed into law last year by President Donald Trump, included the largest reductions in U.S. history to food assistance and health care programs. Its intentionally punitive and retaliatory cuts to California’s Medicaid program, Medi-Cal, are projected to cost the state billions of dollars per year and lead to more than a million Californians losing access to health care.
In the Bay Area, these cuts are becoming painful.
As our news organization documented this month, the number of uninsured people in emergency rooms at Santa Clara Valley Healthcare and Alameda Health System has spiked year over year.

Those county-run systems expect to collectively lose more than a billion dollars annually. Notably, while our systems and residents are scrambling to survive, rural America is receiving a $50 billion lifeline from House Republicans and President Trump to protect their health care systems.
Proposition 40 was written to prop up this state’s safety net in the face of these devastating cuts.
However, this measure is the wrong solution to a real problem.
We advise California voters to reject short-sighted, self-sabotaging Proposition 40.
And we recommend they reject equally myopic Propositions 41 and 42 — countermeasures that would not only nullify the billionaires tax but senselessly shackle the state’s fiscal future.
Killing Golden Goose
Proposition 40 risks long-term pain for short-term gain. It’s the ballot equivalent of eating your seed corn.
Here’s how it would work:
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% levy on the net worth of billionaires who were residents of California on January 1. The tax would be due next year, but the state’s 250 or so billionaires could spread the payments out over five years.
Ninety percent of the revenues raised — estimated anywhere between $40 billion to $100 billion, depending on the expert — would fund health care services. The rest would go toward education and food assistance and administration.
What distinguishes this tax isn’t just that it’s targeting a very base of extremely high-net worth individuals but also that it applies retroactively and taxes wealth, not income.
Wealth taxes are unpopular with many economists, including liberal ones, for several reasons:
They can force the sale of productive assets (e.g. stock shares, patents, copyrights, farmland, etc). They’re difficult to administer because determining the value of some intangible assets, unlike income, is more art than a science. And most injuriously, they can encourage capital flight, especially when executed by a state acting alone.
To be sure, the capital hasn’t fled California yet, but the capitalists have been.
Founders of some of Silicon Valley’s largest companies, including Sergey Brin, Larry Page, Peter Thiel, Mark Zuckerberg and Travis Kalanick, have changed their residencies or announced plans to cut ties with the state in one way or another.
What makes Proposition 40 so dangerously self-destructive is California’s extraordinary dependence upon taxing high-income earners. Over the last two decades, the top 1% of earners have paid approximately 45% of the state’s income taxes.
For that reason, the state’s most respected, nonpartisan authority on policy, the Legislative Analyst’s Office, forecasts short-term benefits but long-term costs:
California will “probably collect tens of billions of dollars from the wealth tax,” according to the LAO. But those gains would likely be temporary.
That’s because the LAO worries that “billionaires may respond to a new wealth tax in ways that reduce their income tax payments. For example, some billionaires may decide to leave California. The income taxes they currently pay to the state also would go away.”
In fact, the LAO projects that billionaires leaving the state would reduce the state’s General Fund revenues by “less than a billion per year.”
But the union that pushed this proposition — Services Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West — wants to gamble.
Its leaders created this to help themselves first and foremost, even at the expense of their typical allies. Opposition to this proposition includes the California Teachers Association, the Association of California School Administrators and the California Professional Firefighters, among several other public and private sector unions. These unions know they’ll suffer when the state’s General Fund takes a hit.
Even the liberal governor of this state is fiercely opposed.
“We can’t let a single advocacy organization, however well-intentioned, write the state’s tax code on its own terms,” said Gov. Gavin Newsom.
We couldn’t agree more.
Self-shackling
To counter Proposition 40, Building a Better California — a political action committee formed earlier this year and backed by Silicon Valley billionaires including Sergey Brin, Vinod Khosla and Eric Scmidt — created two countermeasures, Propositions 41 and 42.
If either Proposition 41 or 42 receives more votes than Proposition 40, the billionaires tax won’t take effect.
The problem is that these two propositions would do far more than nullify the billionaires tax. They would tie the hands of the state far into the future in ways we cannot abide.
Proposition 41
This initiative’s requirement for more audits could be valuable. It would mandate that the State Auditor scrutinize special taxes before they appear on the ballot as well as ongoing programs funded by special taxes. The LAO sees possible savings if the auditor’s recommendations are followed.
However, the problem with Proposition 41 is its second provision. It would prevent any new special taxes from being excluded from the “Gann Limit” — a strict state spending cap enacted in 1979. That means that voters could approve a new tax to address a pressing public need, only to discover that the state cannot spend the money it collects without being constrained by a constitutional limit written half a century ago.

Successive waves of federal cuts to California’s safety net are hitting our shores — and hospitals.
H.R. 1 (aka the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act”), the spending plan written by House Republicans and signed into law last year by President Donald Trump, included the largest reductions in U.S. history to food assistance and health care programs. Its intentionally punitive and retaliatory cuts to California’s Medicaid program, Medi-Cal, are projected to cost the state billions of dollars per year and lead to more than a million Californians losing access to health care.
In the Bay Area, these cuts are becoming painful.
As our news organization documented this month, the number of uninsured people in emergency rooms at Santa Clara Valley Healthcare and Alameda Health System has spiked year over year.

Those county-run systems expect to collectively lose more than a billion dollars annually. Notably, while our systems and residents are scrambling to survive, rural America is receiving a $50 billion lifeline from House Republicans and President Trump to protect their health care systems.
Proposition 40 was written to prop up this state’s safety net in the face of these devastating cuts.
However, this measure is the wrong solution to a real problem.
We advise California voters to reject short-sighted, self-sabotaging Proposition 40.
And we recommend they reject equally myopic Propositions 41 and 42 — countermeasures that would not only nullify the billionaires tax but senselessly shackle the state’s fiscal future.
Killing Golden Goose
Proposition 40 risks long-term pain for short-term gain. It’s the ballot equivalent of eating your seed corn.
Here’s how it would work:
Proposition 40 would impose a one-time 5% levy on the net worth of billionaires who were residents of California on January 1. The tax would be due next year, but the state’s 250 or so billionaires could spread the payments out over five years.
Ninety percent of the revenues raised — estimated anywhere between $40 billion to $100 billion, depending on the expert — would fund health care services. The rest would go toward education and food assistance and administration.
What distinguishes this tax isn’t just that it’s targeting a very base of extremely high-net worth individuals but also that it applies retroactively and taxes wealth, not income.
Wealth taxes are unpopular with many economists, including liberal ones, for several reasons:
They can force the sale of productive assets (e.g. stock shares, patents, copyrights, farmland, etc). They’re difficult to administer because determining the value of some intangible assets, unlike income, is more art than a science. And most injuriously, they can encourage capital flight, especially when executed by a state acting alone.
To be sure, the capital hasn’t fled California yet, but the capitalists have been.
Founders of some of Silicon Valley’s largest companies, including Sergey Brin, Larry Page, Peter Thiel, Mark Zuckerberg and Travis Kalanick, have changed their residencies or announced plans to cut ties with the state in one way or another.
What makes Proposition 40 so dangerously self-destructive is California’s extraordinary dependence upon taxing high-income earners. Over the last two decades, the top 1% of earners have paid approximately 45% of the state’s income taxes.
For that reason, the state’s most respected, nonpartisan authority on policy, the Legislative Analyst’s Office, forecasts short-term benefits but long-term costs:
California will “probably collect tens of billions of dollars from the wealth tax,” according to the LAO. But those gains would likely be temporary.
That’s because the LAO worries that “billionaires may respond to a new wealth tax in ways that reduce their income tax payments. For example, some billionaires may decide to leave California. The income taxes they currently pay to the state also would go away.”
In fact, the LAO projects that billionaires leaving the state would reduce the state’s General Fund revenues by “less than a billion per year.”
But the union that pushed this proposition — Services Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West — wants to gamble.
Its leaders created this to help themselves first and foremost, even at the expense of their typical allies. Opposition to this proposition includes the California Teachers Association, the Association of California School Administrators and the California Professional Firefighters, among several other public and private sector unions. These unions know they’ll suffer when the state’s General Fund takes a hit.
Even the liberal governor of this state is fiercely opposed.
“We can’t let a single advocacy organization, however well-intentioned, write the state’s tax code on its own terms,” said Gov. Gavin Newsom.
We couldn’t agree more.
Self-shackling
To counter Proposition 40, Building a Better California — a political action committee formed earlier this year and backed by Silicon Valley billionaires including Sergey Brin, Vinod Khosla and Eric Scmidt — created two countermeasures, Propositions 41 and 42.
If either Proposition 41 or 42 receives more votes than Proposition 40, the billionaires tax won’t take effect.
The problem is that these two propositions would do far more than nullify the billionaires tax. They would tie the hands of the state far into the future in ways we cannot abide.
Proposition 41
This initiative’s requirement for more audits could be valuable. It would mandate that the State Auditor scrutinize special taxes before they appear on the ballot as well as ongoing programs funded by special taxes. The LAO sees possible savings if the auditor’s recommendations are followed.
However, the problem with Proposition 41 is its second provision. It would prevent any new special taxes from being excluded from the “Gann Limit” — a strict state spending cap enacted in 1979. That means that voters could approve a new tax to address a pressing public need, only to discover that the state cannot spend the money it collects without being constrained by a constitutional limit written half a century ago.

Research will focus on Gann Limit implications, editorial consensus, League of Women Voters position, audit requirements, and potential impacts on MCO tax and hospital fees.

Proposition 41 mandates pre-election audits of programs receiving special tax funds. The State Auditor must identify at least a 10% annual cost reduction and publish the findings in the voter guide.

Proposition 41 also requires four-year audits of programs funded by special taxes passed after January 2026. It prohibits the state from collecting any tax exempted from the Gann Limit after that date. A conflict clause would nullify any competing measure, including Prop 40, if it receives more votes. Because this is a constitutional amendment, it is extremely difficult to reverse.

The Gann Limit caps state spending at 1978-79 levels adjusted for population and inflation. Excess spending over two consecutive years must be split between taxpayer refunds and K-14 education.

Proposition 41 would bar new dedicated taxes from being exempted from the Gann Limit after January 2026. This would prevent voter-approved revenue from crowding out existing programs or triggering refunds instead of funding intended purposes.

The ban on Gann Limit exemptions would affect any state tax, not just special taxes. Reauthorized taxes such as the MCO tax and Hospital Quality Assurance Fee could be at risk if reauthorized after January 2026 while remaining excluded from the limit. These programs draw down billions in federal Medi-Cal matching funds.

Future voter-approved taxes for specific purposes would lose their exemption from the spending cap. Funds could be refunded or diverted instead of spent on their intended purpose. The audit provisions are mixed.

The mandatory 10% cut requirement would bias audits toward predetermined waste conclusions rather than independent assessments. Pre-election audits triggered at 25% of signatures would burden the General Fund with costs for measures that may never qualify or pass. Auditing programs that do not yet exist or are newly created by the tax is also awkward.

Ongoing audits would drain dedicated tax revenues to fund audit bureaucracy. The State Auditor already audits high-risk programs, so the new mandate is redundant and selective rather than comprehensive. The mandatory 10% cut findings could be weaponized in future campaigns to undermine special tax initiatives.

Proposition 41 was largely funded by billionaire PACs including Building a Better California, which spent nearly $58 million to nullify Prop 40. The measure’s transparency framing barely mentions the Gann Limit kill switch that would invalidate Prop 40.

Editorial support is split. The San Diego Union-Tribune, Orange County Register, and San Luis Obispo Tribune support the measure. The Sacramento Bee, San Francisco Chronicle, and Mercury News oppose it.

The Mercury News explicitly votes no on Prop 41, 40, and 42. The League of Women Voters, California Democratic Party, and California State PTA oppose the measure. The Republican Party, Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association, and business groups such as the California Chamber of Commerce and CalTax support it. I will now review nonpartisan analysis from the LA Times and Ballotpedia.

I am weighing the audit provisions against their transparency value. The mandatory 10% cut recommendation is a constitutional political framing device rather than neutral auditing. I will now review PPIC and academic analysis of the Gann Limit.

The audit mandate only targets new special taxes, not existing state spending where waste actually occurs. It therefore fails to address the homelessness spending problem that proponents cite.

The Gann Limit itself is the more serious issue. It is a 1979 formula that has repeatedly forced awkward exclusions because it does not track actual needs such as an aging population, healthcare costs, or federal matching requirements.

The measure would also ban any new state tax from being exempted from the Gann Limit, not just special taxes. This creates a structural fiscal constraint that could nullify voter-approved revenue even when voters explicitly intend it for a dedicated purpose. Taxes passed on the same ballot after January 2026 would be unenforceable.

Proposition 41 is a constitutional poison pill. It was designed to kill Prop 40 while permanently constraining state fiscal policy far beyond that single tax fight.

Opposing Prop 40 does not justify this broader structural change. The billionaire tax itself has serious flaws, including capital flight, valuation disputes, and legal vulnerability. A direct no vote on Prop 40 would be the appropriate response.

The conflict clause would nullify an entire competing measure rather than just the conflicting provisions. This makes it a winner-take-all poison pill.

Future well-designed taxes, such as dedicated climate or education funding, would also be trapped by the permanent ban on Gann Limit exemptions.

Article XIII B Section 4 allows voters to change the appropriations limit for up to four years. This means any new or existing entity of government may establish or modify its limit through direct voter action.

Proposition 41 defines "exempted" to include increases in the state appropriations limit by statute under Article XIII B Section 4. That section allows direct voter action, not just legislative changes. The definition appears poorly drafted.

Section 3(a) bars any state tax taking effect on or after January 1, 2026, from being exempted from the Gann Limit. Section 3(b) would make such taxes unenforceable. Many existing special funds are already excluded by depositing revenue outside the General Fund in separate accounts whose appropriations are not counted. Examples include Prop 98, certain transportation taxes, and tobacco taxes.

The Budget Center notes the MCO tax risk is uncertain and would be litigated, but the stakes are billions in federal matching funds. I am now leaning strongly toward a no vote.

The Southern California News Group editorial boards support the measure even on its own, citing high taxes and spending growth, reasonable pre-tax audits, and the discipline of applying new revenues to the Gann Limit. This is a valid rationale for a yes vote if the goal is to block Prop 40 while also tightening spending limits and increasing audit oversight.

The measure is overbroad for a transparency initiative. Constitutional amendments should be clean and durable, not designed as ballot gamesmanship.

The Gann Limit has well-documented flaws. It nearly forced spending cuts in 2021-22 when revenues surged, forcing the state to use exclusions and one-time spending to avoid hitting the cap. When the limit binds, it does not distinguish good spending from bad.

Mandatory 10% savings recommendations are not genuine auditing. The winner-take-all conflict clause is anti-democratic because it prevents voters from deciding Prop 40 on its own merits.

The transparency goal is only partially achieved. Existing State Auditor authority could be expanded by statute without a constitutional amendment. The 10% mandate undermines auditor independence and the pre-qualification trigger is wasteful.

Proponents claim Gann Limit exemptions let spending spiral and reduce refunds. That is true as a mechanical description.

The Gann Limit’s inflation adjustment tracks per capita personal income, which often grows slower than healthcare, education, and aging costs. When the limit binds, excess revenues are split equally between taxpayer rebates and education, not returned progressively or targeted to the purpose voters approved. Existing categorical exclusions for capital outlay, debt service, and federal mandates are preserved; only new taxes would lose that protection.

How the Gann Limit Threatens Ongoing Investments for Californians
December 2022 | By Kayla Kitson (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/kayla-kitson/), Scott Graves (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/scott-graves/), and Jonathan Kaplan
Print Q&A
Building a just and equitable California for every person no matter their race, ethnicity, gender, age, or zip code requires investments to create health, housing, economic, and educational opportunities. But an archaic spending limit approved by some California voters under a 1979 ballot measure challenges our state’s ability to meet the ongoing needs of Californians. Known by many names — the spending cap, appropriations limit, or Gann Limit — this convoluted budget constraint blocks the state’s ability to build a better and more equitable future.
This Gann Limit Q&A addresses top questions on the spending cap and why California leaders and voters need to rethink the disco-era measure to create healthy, thriving communities for all Californians.
Jump To:
What are the origins of the Gann Limit?
How does the Gann Limit work?
Why does this spending limit matter today?
How does the Gann Limit threaten ongoing investments to help Californians thrive?
Does the Gann Limit affect local governments and school districts?
What can state leaders do about the Gann Limit?
1. What are the origins of the Gann Limit?
The Gann Limit is a constitutional spending cap approved by voters via Proposition 4 in a 1979 special election. Prop. 4 emerged from California’s anti-tax movement of the 1970s. The measure’s key proponent, Paul Gann, also co-authored Prop. 13 — the 1978 initiative that severely restricted property taxes and drastically limited the ability of local jurisdictions to raise revenues for education and community services such as libraries, parks, and fire protection.
Prop. 4 and Prop. 13 were approved by a majority-white electorate during a time when the state’s population was becoming more diverse and white Californians’ support for robust public services was in decline (https://stateofresistancebook.com/articles/prop13).
2. How does the Gann Limit work?
The Gann Limit applies to both state spending and, as explained in question #5, spending by local governments and school districts. At the state level, the limit is based on California’s 1978-79 spending level, which is then adjusted each year for changes in population and per capita personal income. In essence, the Gann Limit enshrined into the state’s Constitution the budget priorities of the late 1970s — even though the needs of Californians have dramatically changed since the disco era.
If revenues exceed the limit over a two-year period, state policymakers must provide half of the revenue over that limit to taxpayers and the other half to K-14 education. Policymakers have some discretion over how to distribute the portion going to taxpayers. In contrast, the portion going to K-14 education must be distributed on a per-pupil basis, which is an inequitable approach that treats all schools the same regardless of their students’ needs.
Alternatively, policymakers have limited options to structure budgets to avoid going over the limit, as explained in question #6. In either case, state leaders lose the flexibility to spend revenues in ways that address critical ongoing needs of Californians, including health care, child care, and housing assistance. For an in-depth explanation of how the Gann Limit works, see this April 2021 report (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4416) by the Legislative Analyst’s Office.
3. Why does this spending limit matter today?
For most of the last two decades, state revenues were far enough below the Gann Limit that it did not have a significant impact on budgeting decisions. However, when the state’s revenues grow faster than population and personal income, as they have in recent years, the Gann Limit comes into play and dictates how a large share of the budget can be spent.
Big revenue gains primarily come from personal income taxes paid by high-income households, who experience much faster income growth than the typical Californian, and who pay higher tax rates under the state’s progressive income tax system (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/californias-tax-revenue-system-isnt-fair-for-all/). While there will be years when the Gann Limit is less of a factor in state budget decisions, over the long run the spending cap will likely continue to impose budget constraints to the extent that state revenues grow faster than the limit itself, as has been the case historically (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4646).
4. How does the Gann Limit threaten ongoing investments to help Californians thrive?
The Gann Limit challenges California’s ability to maintain current service levels and to raise revenues to make bold new investments to help more Californians prosper.
The Gann Limit is just one of several budget formulas in the state Constitution (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/dollars-and-democracy-a-guide-to-the-state-budget-process-2019/) that dictate how revenues can be spent. Prop. 98, approved by voters in 1988, creates a guaranteed annual minimum funding level for K-14 education. Prop. 2 (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-2-should-california-prioritize-paying-down-debt-and-significantly-change-state-budget-reserve-policies/), approved by voters in 2014, requires the state to direct some revenues to paying down debts and adding to the state’s main budget reserve (the Budget Stabilization Account). When revenues exceed the Gann Limit, each dollar above the limit must meet all three requirements: Gann, Prop. 98, and Prop. 2. This means that each $1 of “excess” revenue results in more than $1 in state budget obligations (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4515). Addressing all three obligations could force state leaders to cut public services outside of K-14 education, such as health care, child care, and cash assistance as well as the state university systems.
In addition to undercutting the state’s ability to support current service levels, the spending cap, if left unchanged, will undermine efforts to raise enough revenue to fund significant new ongoing investments to help all Californians thrive. These include investments to expand affordable child care (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/moving-beyond-relief-for-california-care/), increase pay for child care providers (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/californias-subsidized-child-care-providers-are-overdue-for-pay-raise/), and adequately address the homelessness (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/who-is-experiencing-homelessness-in-california/) and affordable housing (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/who-is-experiencing-housing-hardship-in-california/) crises.
Cutting critical services and failing to address the biggest challenges facing the state would significantly harm Californians with low incomes who may not be able to make ends meet without the help of public supports. Many Californians of color are at particular risk because of historical and ongoing discrimination that has often limited them to low-paying, undervalued jobs and blocked them from opportunities to build wealth.
5. Does the Gann Limit affect local governments and school districts?
The Gann Limit generally applies to local governments — cities, counties, and special districts — as well as to K-12 and community college districts, all of which could be impacted in the years to come. Many school districts regularly exceed their spending caps, although the state is currently able to provide relief to these districts by counting certain district expenditures toward the state’s own limit. In general, few cities or counties are currently at risk of exceeding their limits.
However, in future years, the Gann Limit could put pressure on local budgets, particularly for cities and counties that seek revenue increases to bolster local services like affordable housing, health care, parks, and libraries.
6. What can state leaders do about the Gann Limit?
State leaders have some ability to structure budgets to avoid exceeding the limit in the near term. For example, they can spend more on things that are excluded from the limit, such as:
infrastructure projects, including housing;
emergency response;
tax refunds;
some transfers of state funds to local governments; and
spending to comply with court and federal mandates.
Policymakers can also reduce revenues to avoid going over the limit, such as by expanding tax credits like the California Earned Income Tax Credit and Young Child Tax Credit (https://calbudgetcenter.org/series/what-is-the-california-earned-income-tax-credit/).
Finally, some of the Gann Limit rules are spelled out in state statute rather than in the state Constitution. In these cases, lawmakers have limited opportunities to change the law to ease some Gann Limit pressures. For example, state leaders made some changes in the 2021-22 (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4449) and 2022-23 (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/4631) state budgets to avoid exceeding the limit, including allowing more flexibility in deciding whether to count state funding for local governments under the state or local limits.
However, in the long run, the Gann Limit’s restrictive rules may jeopardize existing services and many kinds of ongoing expenditures, such as big new investments in affordable child care or health care.
Even though a period of weak revenue growth may temporarily keep the state under the spending cap, the Gann Limit will roar back to life when revenues pick up again. In order to address the long-run threats posed by the limit, state leaders should ask California voters to change the state Constitution to modify or eliminate the spending cap. This would allow the state to both support the rising costs of current services and leave room for significant new ongoing investments to address the critical needs of Californians.

Endorsement: Prop 41 is a cynical poison pill. And it isn’t the only one on California’s ballot
Prop 41 is one of two attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the infamous billionaire wealth tax.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 29, 2026
It wouldn’t be a California election without a few petty, revenge-motivated ballot measures.
Proposition 41 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop41-text-proposed-laws.pdf) is one of two poison pill attempts on the November ballot to take out Prop 40, the infamous billionaire wealth tax. The measure explicitly states that even if Prop 40 passes, it would be nullified if Prop 41 or its cousin initiative Prop 42 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/california-proposition-42-taxes-22449389.php) pass with a larger number of votes.
Backed by Building a Better California, a political action committee largely funded by billionaire Google cofounder Sergey Brin (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/billionaire-tax-california-pac-22442333.php), Prop 41 would require new special taxes that raise money for specific purposes to adhere to state spending rules, while mandating regular audits of the programs they fund.
What’s so bad about ensuring California spends tax revenue wisely?
